cards.front: Why must high-level source code be translated before a CPU can run it?
cards.back: A CPU can execute only binary **machine code**, so readable source code must be converted into instructions for a particular processor.
cards.hint: Think about which form of instructions the CPU can actually execute.

cards.front: How does a compiler differ from an interpreter?
cards.back: A **compiler** translates the whole program into a separate executable before it runs. An **interpreter** translates and runs one statement at a time and produces no separate executable.
cards.hint: Compare when the translation happens and whether a separate file is made.

cards.front: What are the six stages of compilation, in order?
cards.back: 1 **lexical analysis** (split into tokens), 2 **syntax analysis** (check grammar, build a tree), 3 **semantic analysis** (check meaning and data types), 4 intermediate code generation (processor-independent), 5 **optimisation** (faster or less memory), 6 **code generation** (final machine code).
cards.hint: Each stage hands its output to the next one.

cards.back: An **assembler** is a translator that converts assembly language into machine code, usually one assembly instruction to one machine instruction.
cards.hint: Assembly language uses short codes such as ADD and LOAD.

cards.front: Is an assembler the same as a compiler?
cards.back: No. An **assembler** works on assembly language, usually one instruction to one instruction, while a compiler translates a whole high-level language program.
cards.hint: Think about the input language each one translates.

cards.front: Does running a compiler also run the program?
cards.back: No. A **compiler** only translates the program. The resulting executable is run afterwards as a separate step.
cards.hint: Consider what files exist after compiling.

cards.front: Why does an interpreted program usually run more slowly?
cards.back: The interpreter translates the source code again every time the program runs, because both the interpreter and the source are needed each run.
cards.hint: Count how many times the translation happens.

cards.back: The source code is split into **tokens**, the smallest meaningful units such as keywords and names. Spaces and comments are discarded.
cards.hint: It is the first compilation stage.

cards.front: Which compilation stage checks that data types match and variables are declared?
cards.back: **Semantic analysis** checks that statements are meaningful, for example that data types match and variables are declared.
cards.hint: This stage checks meaning rather than grammar.

cards.front: Why does a compiler suit finished software?
cards.back: Users can run the **executable** without any translator, and the source code stays private. The executable also usually runs faster.
cards.hint: Think about what the user needs and what the developer wants to protect.

cards.front: Why does an interpreter suit development and learning?
cards.back: A programmer can run a change straight away and see exactly where an error occurs, because errors appear as each statement is reached.
cards.hint: Think about how quickly feedback comes after a change.
